title: CKD -> secondary hyperparathyroidism lab pattern
vignette: A 52-year-old man with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is evaluated in the nephrology clinic. His estimated glomerular filtration rate is 15 mL/min/1.73 m2 (normal >90), consistent with advanced chronic kidney disease. He has no other medical conditions. Which of the following sets of laboratory findings involving parathyroid hormone, calcium, phosphorus, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is most likely present in this patient?

clues.note: ADPKD is a common cause of progressive chronic kidney disease, setting up the mineral disturbances that follow.

clues.text: estimated glomerular filtration rate is 15 mL/min/1.73 m2
clues.note: eGFR 15 / normal >90 = advanced (stage 5) CKD. The failing kidney can neither excrete phosphate nor make 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, triggering the secondary hyperparathyroidism cascade.
The active vitamin D form; the diseased kidney loses 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, so 1,25-diOH vitamin D falls (while the liver-made 25-OH precursor stays normal).

whatMatters: Advanced CKD (eGFR 15) causes CKD-mineral bone disorder / secondary hyperparathyroidism: phosphate retention (↑phosphorus), loss of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (↓1,25-diOH vitamin D, normal 25-OH vitamin D), and consequent HYPOcalcemia (↓Ca) - all of which drive PTH up (↑PTH). Answer A: ↑PTH, ↓Ca, ↑phosphorus, normal 25-OH vitamin D, ↓1,25-diOH vitamin D.
strategy: Trace the CKD mineral cascade: failing kidney -> retains phosphate (↑PO4) and can't make active vitamin D (↓1,25-diOH, normal 25-OH) -> serum calcium falls (↓Ca) -> parathyroids ramp up (↑PTH = secondary hyperPTH). Pick the row with high PTH, low Ca, high phosphorus, normal 25-OH, low 1,25-diOH. Reject rows with high calcium (that's primary/tertiary patterns) or low phosphorus.

options.text: PTH ↑ | Calcium ↓ | Phosphorus ↑ | 25-OH vitamin D normal | 1,25-diOH vitamin D ↓

eliminations.label: ↑PTH, ↑Ca, ↓phosphorus - that's primary hyperparathyroidism
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: high PTH with HIGH calcium and LOW phosphorus. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this is primary hyperparathyroidism (autonomous PTH), not the CKD picture, where calcium is low and phosphorus is retained/high. ✅ Correct if: parathyroid adenoma.

eliminations.label: ↓PTH with low Ca - inappropriate (should be high in CKD)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: low PTH with hypocalcemia. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: hypocalcemia should DRIVE PTH up; low PTH with low calcium indicates hypoparathyroidism, not CKD. ✅ Correct if: primary hypoparathyroidism (e.g., post-thyroidectomy).

eliminations.label: ↑PTH but LOW phosphorus - wrong phosphate direction
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: high PTH, low calcium, but LOW phosphorus. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: in CKD the kidney can't excrete phosphate, so phosphorus is HIGH, not low; low phosphorus fits vitamin D deficiency with intact kidneys. ✅ Correct if: nutritional vitamin D deficiency with normal renal function.

eliminations.label: ↓PTH, ↑Ca - opposite of the CKD cascade
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: low PTH with high calcium. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: CKD causes HIGH PTH and LOW calcium; this pattern is the reverse. ✅ Correct if: hypercalcemia of malignancy/other PTH-independent hypercalcemia.

reasoning: eGFR 15 = advanced CKD (kidney fails its phosphate-excreting and vitamin D-activating roles)
Phosphate retention (↑PO4) + loss of 1-alpha-hydroxylase (↓1,25-diOH vitamin D, normal 25-OH)
Both lower serum calcium (↓Ca), which drives parathyroids -> ↑PTH (secondary hyperPTH)
mechanism: In advanced chronic kidney disease, two failures converge to produce secondary hyperparathyroidism (part of CKD-mineral bone disorder). First, the kidney cannot excrete phosphate, so serum phosphorus rises; phosphate also complexes serum calcium and stimulates FGF-23, which further suppresses calcitriol. Second, the diseased kidney loses 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, so it can no longer convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D (made in the liver, remains normal) to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (falls); low calcitriol reduces intestinal calcium absorption. Both hyperphosphatemia and reduced calcitriol lower serum calcium. Hypocalcemia (sensed by the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor), hyperphosphatemia, and low calcitriol all directly stimulate the parathyroid glands, raising PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism). The net panel: ↑PTH, ↓Ca, ↑phosphorus, normal 25-OH vitamin D, ↓1,25-diOH vitamin D. (Over years, glands can become autonomous -> tertiary hyperparathyroidism with high calcium.)

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Renal/Endo > CKD-MBD / secondary hyperparathyroidism: ↓ renal phosphate excretion (↑PO4), ↓1-alpha-hydroxylase (↓1,25-diOH vit D), ↓Ca -> ↑PTH; contrast primary (↑Ca,↓PO4) and tertiary hyperPTH.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on 1-alpha-hydroxylase, calcitriol (1,25-diOH vit D) vs 25-OH vit D, secondary vs tertiary hyperparathyroidism, or FGF-23? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: High-calcium rows = primary/tertiary hyperPTH; low-phosphorus rows = vitamin D deficiency with intact kidneys; low-PTH rows = hypoparathyroidism.
